## Overview

The Svans (Svan: *შუ̂ანა̈რ*, romanized: *shwanær*; Georgian: *სვანები*, romanized: *svanebi*) are an ethnic subgroup of Georgians indigenous to Svaneti, a region in northwest Georgia. They primarily live in the mountains of Svaneti, including the districts of Mestia and Lentekhi, along the Enguri, Tskhenistsqali and Kodori rivers. Some Svan speakers live in the Kodori Valley of the de facto independent republic of Abkhazia. Estimates for the number of Svan speakers range from 30,000 to 80,000, while the native language is described as being spoken by fewer than 30,000 Svans. Svan and Georgian belong to the Kartvelian language family. The Svans are significant in folk-culture terms because they have retained older traditions, including pre-Christian beliefs, while maintaining a distinct regional language and customary practices.

## Festivals & rituals

The Svans are Georgian Orthodox Christians and were Christianized in the 4th–6th centuries. Some remnants of pre-Christian beliefs have been maintained. Saint George, known as *Jgëræg* to the locals, is a patron saint of Georgia and the most respected saint among the Svans. The sources also state that the Svans have retained old traditions including blood revenge, although this practice has declined over time as law enforcement has taken hold.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Svans speak their own traditionally unwritten language, which has historically been used informally in day-to-day activities. Svan speakers traditionally relied on standard Georgian as their literary language, and through the late 19th century there were no known written Svan grammar books or dictionaries.

## Language & religion

Svan is a Kartvelian language spoken primarily by the Svans in the western Georgian region of Svaneti. It is a spoken regional language with no written standard or official status, and most speakers also speak Georgian. Svan has traditionally been used in familiar and casual social communication, while standard Georgian served as the literary language. The language is considered endangered, and UNESCO designates it as a “definitely endangered language.”

Svan is divided into Upper Svan and Lower Svan. Upper Svan includes the Upper Bal and Lower Bal dialects. Upper Bal includes Ushguli, Kala, Ipar, Mulakh, Mestia, Lenzer and Latal; Lower Bal includes Becho, Tskhumar, Etser, Par, Chubekh and Lakham. Lower Svan includes Lashkhian, represented by Lashkh, and Lentekhian, including Lentekhi, Kheled, Khopur, Rtskhmelur and Cholur.

Svan is the most differentiated of the four Kartvelian languages and is believed to have split off in the 2nd millennium BC or earlier. It has retained features lost in other Kartvelian languages, including the voiceless aspirated uvular plosive /qʰ/ and the glides /w/ and /j/. The Upper Bal dialect has 18 vowels. Svan has an alphabet similar to the Mingrelian alphabet, with additional letters otherwise obsolete in the Georgian script.

The Svans are Georgian Orthodox Christians. They were Christianized in the 4th–6th centuries, while some pre-Christian beliefs remain. Saint George, or *Jgëræg*, is especially respected.
